items.prompt: Define earnings from work.
items.canonical_answer: Monetary rewards received from work over a stated period, depending on the relevant payment arrangements.
marking_guidance: Meaning: monetary work rewards 1; qualifier: stated period/arrangements 1.

items.prompt: Explain how rising orders can affect technician earnings when suitably trained applicants are scarce.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: employers need more technician labour (1); competition for scarce skills may make firms offer higher pay to recruit or retain workers (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change 1; mechanism/effect for firm: demand relative to scarce supply raises recruitment pressure 1.

items.prompt: Explain why two workers with the same hourly rate can have different monthly earnings.
items.canonical_answer: They may work different paid hours (1), so equal pay per hour can generate different totals over the month (1).
marking_guidance: Context: equal rate; reasoning: hours differ 1; result: monthly totals differ 1.

items.prompt: Explain why subtracting tax to find disposable income does not by itself calculate real income.
items.canonical_answer: Disposable income adjusts for relevant taxes and deductions (1), while real income requires adjustment for the price level to measure purchasing power (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: deduction versus price adjustment; boundary/test: tax basis versus price index, 1 each.

items.prompt: Define an earnings differential.
items.canonical_answer: A difference in rewards between workers or groups measured on a comparable basis.
marking_guidance: Definition: reward difference 1; qualifier: comparable worker/group basis 1.

items.prompt: Explain why a difference in group average monthly earnings does not show that each worker in one group earns more than each in the other.
items.canonical_answer: An average summarises the group rather than each member (1), whereas individual earnings can overlap across the groups (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: group summary versus individual distribution, 1 each.

items.prompt: Explain why longer paid hours could contribute to a group’s higher monthly earnings without a higher hourly rate.
items.canonical_answer: More hours multiply the same hourly reward over a larger period of work (1), so the monthly total can be higher despite equal rates (1).
marking_guidance: Context: monthly gap; reasoning: hours-times-rate 1; result: higher total without rate gap 1.

items.prompt: Define nominal earnings.
items.canonical_answer: Monetary rewards measured in current money without adjustment for price changes.

items.prompt: Explain how expanding training opportunities can affect earnings in an occupation when employer demand is unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: more people can acquire the relevant skills (1); a larger available labour supply may reduce firms’ pressure to offer higher pay, other conditions unchanged (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change: training supply 1; mechanism/effect for firm: more available skills can ease wage pressure 1.

items.prompt: Explain why a 10 percent nominal pay rise with a price index rising from 100 to 110 need not increase real pay.
items.canonical_answer: Prices rise by the same proportion as monetary pay (1), so dividing new pay by the index ratio leaves purchasing power unchanged in this example (1).
marking_guidance: Context: matched changes; reasoning: price adjustment 1; result: unchanged real reward 1.

items.prompt: Define the total reward decomposition into transfer earnings and economic rent.
items.canonical_answer: Actual factor reward equals the minimum needed to retain it in the current use plus any amount above that minimum.
marking_guidance: Definition: total split 1; qualifier: retention threshold plus excess 1.

items.prompt: Explain how a factor’s retention minimum differs from the economic rent in its reward.
items.canonical_answer: Transfer earnings are the retention minimum (1), whereas economic rent is the excess of the actual reward above that minimum (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: minimum versus excess, 1 each.

items.prompt: Explain the division of N$9,000 monthly reward where the stated minimum needed to retain the worker is N$7,200.
items.canonical_answer: N$7,200 is transfer earnings (1); the remaining N$1,800 is economic rent because it exceeds the retention minimum (1).

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling the N$2,000 above a worker’s N$6,000 retention minimum transfer earnings when actual pay is N$8,000.

items.prompt: An invented regional labour report compares monthly earnings in two occupations. Repair technicians average N$8,000 and packing staff N$5,600. Technician jobs require training with few qualified applicants. Packing hours vary seasonally. The report supplies no comparable hourly rates or individual distributions. (a) Describe three relevant features (6). (b) Examine possible explanations of the gap (7). (c) Suggest how the comparison should be improved before drawing conclusions about individual pay (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Technicians’ average is N$2,400 higher. Training limits immediate availability of qualified applicants. Packing hours vary, which can affect monthly earnings. (b) Scarce demanded skills can support recruitment pressure and higher rates. Different paid hours can also affect the average monthly total. The gap may reflect composition and experience as well as skill, so the data do not isolate a single cause or show every technician earns more than every packer. (c) Compare hourly rates and paid hours on consistent terms, then examine qualifications, experience and responsibilities. Inspect individual distributions to see overlap and avoid using a group mean as an individual prediction. The judgement should distinguish a descriptive gap from an evidenced causal explanation; current figures support hypotheses rather than a complete attribution.
marking_guidance: Context: regional report. Parts/allocation: (a) gap, training, seasonal hours, 2 each = 6. (b) skill-scarcity mechanism 3, hours effect 2, attribution/individual limits 2 = 7. (c) common basis 2, relevant characteristics 2, distribution/evidence judgement 3 = 7.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: (a) Define earnings (2). (b) Define an earnings differential (2). (c) Explain why real and disposable income differ (2). (d) Explain why a skilled occupation may attract higher pay (2). (e) Explain why ownership sector alone does not determine pay (2). (f) Explain why seasonal hours can affect annual earnings (2). (g) Explain economic rent using a retention minimum (2). (h) Explain why a gender average gap alone does not establish its cause (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Monetary work reward over a stated period. (b) Difference between comparable worker/group rewards. (c) Real adjusts for prices; disposable for taxes/deductions. (d) Required expertise can be scarce relative to employer demand, supporting higher offers. (e) Both sectors contain varied jobs and conditions, so the label does not isolate a rate difference. (f) Fewer paid weeks can lower annual total even at the same hourly rate. (g) It is the reward above the minimum needed to retain the factor. (h) Hours, job mix, access and discrimination are possible influences; a raw average does not separate them.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2 each. (a) work reward + period; (b) difference + common basis; (c) two distinct adjustments; (d) scarce skill + employer demand; (e) varied jobs + no fixed ranking; (f) paid time + total effect; (g) excess + retention threshold; (h) possible factors + attribution limit.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: An invented technician receives N$10,000 monthly and would remain in the stated current use for a minimum N$8,000. New training could increase the number of qualified applicants. The technician’s nominal pay later rises to N$10,500 while the price index rises from 100 to 105. (a) Define transfer earnings (2). (b) Explain the original reward split (4). (c) Explain how the training and price changes affect the earnings analysis (7). (d) Discuss whether higher nominal pay alone proves the technician is better off (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Minimum reward needed to retain a factor in current use. (b) N$8,000 is the retention minimum; N$2,000 is economic rent, the excess above it. Together they equal N$10,000. (c) More qualified applicants can expand labour supply, easing scarcity-related wage pressure if demand is unchanged. Exact real later pay is N$10,500 divided by 105 times 100 = N$10,000 at base prices, so purchasing power is unchanged in this comparison. The new retention minimum is not supplied, so the later rent split cannot be calculated. (d) Higher money earnings may help meet nominal obligations, but matched price growth means no measured purchasing-power gain. Deductions, hours and non-wage conditions could also change and are absent. The supported judgement is that nominal growth alone is insufficient: assess real resources and relevant conditions without inventing changes or assuming the original retention threshold persists.
marking_guidance: Context: technician. Parts/allocation: (a) minimum 1, current-use qualifier 1. (b) minimum identified/explained 2, excess identified/explained 2 = 4. (c) labour-supply mechanism 3, exact deflation and interpretation 3, missing new threshold 1 = 7. (d) nominal consideration 2, real/other-condition limits 2, supported evidence judgement 3 = 7.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an invented teacher should explain differences in average earnings between agriculture, manufacturing and services solely as differences in workers’ skills when hours and job composition are not supplied (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: different skill requirements and scarce expertise can affect labour supply and employer demand, helping explain reward differences. Against: sectors contain varied occupations, and paid hours, seasonality, productivity, bargaining and composition also matter. An average does not show each person’s pay or isolate skills. Judgement: treat skills as one possible mechanism and seek comparable rates, hours and job evidence before attributing the gap. The condition for a strong skill explanation is evidence that relevant skill differences account for the comparison after other important circumstances are considered. Sector labels and raw averages alone do not meet it.
marking_guidance: Argument for: skill demand/supply mechanism developed, up to 4. Argument against: alternative factors and average/individual limits developed, up to 4. Judgement: distinct comparable-evidence condition, 1. Total 9.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
